newsitem.title: IRAN: Importers drive Iran rial weaker ahead of polls.
newsitem.headline: Importers drive Iran rial weaker ahead of polls.

text.p: The Iranian rial currency has weakened on the Tehran black market ahead of presidential elections on Friday, but unofficial money changers said on Wednesday the fall was due to strong importer demand.
The rial was offered by unauthorised street dealers at 4,800 to the dollar, compared to the official rate of 3,000 rials.

"It has not got that much to do with the election. It is more to do with a major importer needing dollars...This is the biggest fall this year," one said, referring to the Iranian year which started on March 21.
"The rate was 4,700 rials last week," said another trader, his jeans and shirt pockets stuffed with dog-eared dollar and rial bills.
Iranians go to the polls on Friday to select one of four candidates who will succeed President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.
Rates offered by traders on Tehran's Jomhuri Street are one of the better signals of inflationary expectations among people in this city of seven million and its appetite for imports.
Inflation is officially assessed at around 25 percent, compared to 50 percent in recent years, and together with high unemployment is the main economic complaint of most Iranians.
In January the rial was worth 4,600 per dollar on the black market. In early April it slipped to 4,750 on high demand by pilgrims leaving for the annual haj pilgrimage in Saudi Arabia.
State banks only sell Iranian travellers limited amounts of foreign exchange at the official rate.
The Iranian government has tried to maintain stability in the value of the rial to slow inflation. It has also clamped down on money changers, but evidently without complete success.

U.S. sanctions against Iran helped precipitate a near free-fall in the value of the currency in 1995 to around 7,000 per dollar before the government imposed strict export currency regulations and arrested street money changers.
Responsibility for eradicating black market dealings was turned over to the intelligence service from the police.
Since then the unofficial rate has held below 5,000, but analysts said a pickup in inflation or any renewed U.S. action against Iran would put further pressure on the rate.

Tehran's government uses two official exchange rates. A rate of 1,750 rials against the dollar is still used for some budget allocations and a rate of 3,000 is used for all other government-sanctioned transactions.

Disparities between the two government rates and the value on the illegal market have meant profits for those who can take advantage of buying dollars at the lower rate of 3,000 or even 1,750 and changing them on the street.

"There are so many people who can make a fortune by just doing nothing, by doing no real business. That is why industry can't attract proper investment...It's just wheeler-dealing," said one diplomat in Tehran.
Rafsanjani had attempted but failed to unify the country's exchange rates to make the rial fully convertible.

The leading contender in this week's presidential polls, parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, wrote in his campaign literature: "We must move toward stabilisation and consolidation of the purchasing power of our national currency."
